title: Read to the sick
hook: ten perceptions read to the sick monk Girimananda, who recovers

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eleven blessings of metta, and your line, wish one person well. How was the night? Today, a new week, and a different bedside: someone who is ill. Day six hundred seventy-three.

When someone we love is sick, we bring things. Soup, flowers, a phone charger, a magazine nobody reads. What we really want to bring is something that helps, and we often don't know what that is. In the Book of Tens, a monk named Girimananda is sick, in pain, gravely ill. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, comes to the Buddha and asks him to visit, out of compassion. The Buddha does something unexpected. He doesn't go himself. He sends Ananda back with something to bring. Not medicine. A list of ten things to read aloud. Today: sanna.
screen: `WHAT DO WE BRING THE SICK?` → `GIRIMANANDA IS GRAVELY ILL.` → `ANANDA IS SENT WITH A LIST.`

segments.voice: If you go to Girimananda, the Buddha says, and tell him the ten perceptions, it's possible his illness will subside at once. Then he gives them. One, impermanence: the body, feelings, all of it, changing. Two, not-self: none of it is me or mine. Three, the unattractive: the body seen plainly, hair, skin, bones, the inside as well as the outside. Four, drawbacks: the body as a home for many illnesses, and the text names a long list of them, eye disease to fever. Five, abandoning: letting go of harmful thoughts. Six, dispassion. Seven, cessation. Eight, not delighting in the whole world. Nine, the impermanence of all that's made. And ten, mindfulness of breathing, given in full: breathing in long, breathing out long, and on through sixteen steps. Ananda learns them, goes to Girimananda, and recites them. And the text says Girimananda recovered from that illness. Notice what kind of list this is. It isn't comforting in the usual way. It doesn't say you'll be fine. It looks straight at the body, its fragility and its changes, and ends with the simplest thing a sick person can still do: breathe, and know they're breathing. One modern reading is that a mind steadied and less gripped by fear helps the body. The text itself doesn't explain it. It just says he recovered. In some Theravada communities, this sutta is still chanted for people who are ill.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SENDS ANANDA.` · `IMPERMANENCE, NOT-SELF.` · `ENDING WITH THE BREATH.` · then, large: `HE RECOVERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read something kind to someone ill. Sit, and settle with the tenth perception, the breath. Breathing in long, know it. Breathing out long, know it. Now bring to mind someone who is unwell, near or far. Picture sitting beside them. What could you read or say that would steady them? A favorite line, a message, a memory. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. Choose one thing, and plan to send it today. The bell holds the time.

sanna. The Pali word for perception, as in the ten perceptions Ananda carries to Girimananda's bedside in the Book of Tens, from impermanence to mindfulness of breathing, after which the monk recovers. Today's word.
Your line: ten perceptions. Today, send one steadying word to someone who's unwell, and take one long, known breath for them. Day six hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: In parts of the Theravada world, monks chant the Girimananda Sutta for the sick, and visiting and reading to ill people, lay or ordained, is a long-standing Buddhist act of care.

original.note: Pali sanna: perception, recognition; the ten sanna are the ten perceptions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sick person needs only comfort.
what it means: the Buddha sent a sick monk ten clear-eyed perceptions, ending with the breath.
what a scholar hears: the fourth perception names dozens of diseases one by one, from eye disease to fever; the tenth gives the same sixteen breathing steps as MN 118.

notes: AN 10.60 paraphrased. Confirm the order of the ten perceptions and that the tenth gives the sixteen steps of anapanasati.
'Many teachers read the healing this way' is a general characterization; the text gives no mechanism.
Confirm that the Girimananda Sutta is chanted for the sick in some Theravada communities (it is included in some paritta collections).
The practice includes 'if you pray, you can hold them in prayer'; no prayer text is given.

Audit (second sample): replaced the vague 'many teachers read the healing this way' with a reading marked as one modern interpretation, and the trapdoor's unsourced 'one of the canon's longest medical lists' with checkable details.
